passage:
Dear Joseph,

You'll laugh, but I finally went to the electricity office about the meter shift. The clerk said the file could take months, then lowered a voice and murmured that "a little something" would move it by evening. The only way, apparently. My hand actually went to my purse.

Then I remembered what you once said, that small bribes are practical today and keep alive a system that will let you down tomorrow. So I said, "I'll wait, thank you. Could I meet the section head?" The clerk shrugged. The section head checked the file and said it would be cleared in a few days. I've also put in a request through the online portal and sent an RTI asking about the delay.

It moved without money, though slower, and I'm still irritated. Wish me patience.

Anjali

qa.q: What did the clerk say would move the file by evening?
qa.a: The clerk murmured that "a little something" would move it by evening.

qa.q: Why did Anjali's hand go to the purse, and what made it stop?
qa.a: The wish to get the file moving made Anjali's hand go to the purse, but remembering Joseph's remark that small bribes keep alive a system that lets people down stopped it.

qa.q: What could Anjali do if the file stalls again?
qa.a: Follow up with the section head, check the online portal request, and use the RTI to ask for reasons for the delay.

qa.q: How might the clerk see Anjali's refusal?
qa.a: The clerk may find it unusual, since asking for "a little something" was presented as the only way, though Anjali stayed polite and simply moved to the section head.

grounding: Speed money is offered as the only way; Anjali recognises the ask, declines politely and escalates to the section head and the portal.

passage: "So, Francis, you asked why I spent six weeks on a birth certificate. I'm Baljeet. The clerk at the municipal office in Ludhiana said, 'Three months normally. Five hundred rupees and it's ready tomorrow.' He said it like it was the only way. And honestly, it felt practical. Five hundred is nothing, right? But I thought about my mother, who paid 'speed money' for her pension file years ago and then had to pay again when a new clerk came. It never ends. So I said, 'No, thank you. I'll wait for the normal process.' He shrugged. I went upstairs to the section officer, calmly, and asked for the timeline in writing. When that didn't move, I filed an RTI asking for the status of my application. Two weeks after the RTI, the certificate came. No bribe. Took longer, but now I know the route."

qa.q: How much did the clerk ask for to speed up the certificate?
What was Baljeet feeling when the clerk made the offer?
qa.a: Baljeet felt tempted, since paying seemed practical, but uneasy remembering the mother's experience with the pension file.

qa.q: How did Baljeet respond to the speed-money request?
qa.a: Baljeet declined politely, went to the section officer for a written timeline, and filed an RTI asking for the application's status.

qa.q: How might the clerk see Baljeet's refusal?
qa.a: The clerk seems indifferent, shrugging, perhaps used to people paying and not expecting anyone to escalate.

grounding: A clerk presents speed money as the only way; the protagonist recognises it, declines politely, escalates to a senior and uses an RTI.

passage:
Week one: Zainab's shop licence renewal had been "under process" at the Bhopal municipal office for two months. The clerk leaned forward. "Madam, if you want it this week, one thousand. Otherwise, who knows." Zainab's face went hot. She wanted the licence. She said, "Let me think."
Week two: Her friend Charu, who volunteered with a citizens' group, came over with tea and a laptop. "Don't pay. It feeds the whole thing." Together they wrote a polite letter to the zonal officer, noting the date of application, and filed a complaint on the municipal grievance portal.
Week five: No reply. Charu helped Zainab file an RTI request asking for the file's status and the reason for delay.
Week eight: The renewed licence arrived by post. Zainab laminated it and taped a copy of the RTI to the back of her shop register, in case she needed the route again.

qa.q: How much did the clerk ask for to speed up the licence?
qa.a: One thousand, to have it that week.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling when the clerk asked for money?
qa.a: She felt angry and pressured, her face going hot, while also wanting the licence badly.

qa.q: What steps did Zainab and Charu take instead of paying?
qa.a: They wrote to the zonal officer, filed a grievance on the portal, and then filed an RTI asking for the file's status.

qa.q: How might Charu see Zainab's temptation to pay?
qa.a: Charu understands it, but believes paying feeds a system that fails people, so she offers practical help instead.

grounding: A clerk asks for speed money; the protagonist declines, escalates to a senior and uses the grievance portal and RTI with a friend's help.
